title: Calvin, Beza, catechisms: define faith by persuasion of God’s goodwill — Molinaeus, Maresius, Alting
source_text: LXXXIV. Ita Calvinus, & Beza, & vulgares quidam Catechismi, fidem describunt solum ab illa fiducia, seu persuasione, quam secum trahit fides salvifica & justificans de gratia Dei, & ejus erga nos benevolentia. Nam Calvino & Bezae, ut supra retulimus, fides justificans est, Divinae erga nos benevolentiae firma certaque cognitio, quae gratiae in Christo promissae veritate fundata, per Spiritum Sanctum revelatur mentibus nostris & cordibus obsignatur. Et brevis quidam Catechismus vulgaris fidem definit esse, Certam fiduciam seu persuasionem, quam debet habere quilibet Christianus, quod Deus Pater ipsum amet, propter Filium suum Jesum Christum. Ad quas definitiones proxime accedit descriptio celeberrimorum virorum, Petri Molinaei, & Samuelis Maresii, & Henrici quoque Altingii. Nam Petro Molinaeo fides est, Firmus assensus promissionibus Evangelii, quo fidelis credit eas non tantum esse veras, sed etiam ad se peculiariter pertinere. Maresio vero, Donum quo promissionibus Evangelii in Christo, tanquam veris & certis acquiescimus, easque nobis fiducialiter applicamus. Denique Altingio, Cognitio gratiae Dei in Christo Redemptore, ejusdemque fiducialis apprehensio, qua quisque fidelis illam sibi singulariter applicat.
pass_a_gloss: Thus Calvin, and Beza, and certain popular Catechisms, describe faith only from that trust, or persuasion, which saving and justifying faith draws with it concerning God's grace and his goodwill toward us. For to Calvin and Beza, as we related above, justifying faith is, A firm and certain knowledge of the divine goodwill toward us, which, founded on the truth of the grace promised in Christ, is revealed to our minds by the Holy Spirit and sealed upon our hearts. And a certain short popular Catechism defines faith to be, A certain trust or persuasion which every Christian ought to have, that God the Father loves him, for his Son Jesus Christ. To which definitions the description of most celebrated men comes nearest — Peter du Moulin, and Samuel Maresius, and Henry Alting also. For to Peter du Moulin faith is, A firm assent to the promises of the Gospel, by which the believer believes them not only to be true, but also to pertain peculiarly to himself. But to Maresius, A gift by which we rest in the promises of the Gospel in Christ as true and certain, and apply them to ourselves trustingly. Finally to Alting, Knowledge of the grace of God in Christ the Redeemer, and a fiducial apprehension of the same, by which each believer applies it to himself singularly.
pass_b_english: Calvin, Beza, and popular catechisms define faith from the fiducia/persuasion of God’s grace and goodwill that saving faith carries.
Calvin/Beza: firm certain knowledge of divine goodwill, founded on grace promised in Christ, revealed and sealed by the Spirit.
Short catechism: sure trust that the Father loves me for Christ.

Near them: du Moulin (firm assent that Gospel promises are true and peculiarly mine); Maresius (gift resting in and fiducially applying those promises); Alting (knowledge plus fiducial apprehension of grace in Christ the Redeemer).
